desc:
Given a binary tree and an integer target, return every root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to target. A path is reported as the list of its node values from the root down to the leaf, and a leaf is a node without children.

Report the paths in left-to-right order of their leaves (the order a pre-order walk that visits the left child first would find them). If no path matches, return an empty list. Different paths may have identical value lists; each path is reported once.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). Node values can be negative in this problem, so a missing child is written as 1000 (real node values always lie between -500 and 500, so the marker can never be confused with a value). The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing 1000 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with 1000. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, 1000, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [5, 4, 8, 11, 1000, 13, 4, 7, 2, 1000, 1000, 5, 1] and target = 22 the answer is [[5, 4, 11, 2], [5, 8, 4, 5]].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, missing child written as 1000, no trailing 1000)
The total number of values in the returned paths is at most 6,000
hints: A path is only valid if it ends at a leaf, so decide at the leaves. What do you need to know when you arrive at one?
Track the running sum from the root to every node. A leaf whose running sum equals target ends a matching path.

Do not copy whole paths while descending. Remember each node's parent, and rebuild the list by walking up from a matching leaf, then reverse it. Visit leaves in pre-order (push the right child before the left child on a stack) so the output order comes out right.
editorial: The running sum of a node (sum of values from the root to it) is computed from its parent's in O(1). A root-to-leaf path matches exactly when its leaf has running sum target, so the problem splits into two parts: find the matching leaves in left-to-right order, and turn each into its value list.

Visiting nodes with an explicit stack in pre-order (push right, then left) meets the leaves in left-to-right order. For every matching leaf, climb the parent links to the root and reverse. Only matching leaves pay for building a path, so the total work is O(n + total output length) instead of O(n · depth) when paths are copied at every node.
Because values may be negative, you can never prune a branch just because its running sum already exceeds the target.
